h1: AC Bill Calculator Pakistan: What an AC Adds to Your Bill
author: ali-ahmad

outputs.label: Extra on your bill a month
Real cost of each AC unit
Penalty on the next bills without the AC

answer: A {{out.ac_name|raw}} running {{in.hours|int}} hours a day adds about {{out.ac_units|int}} units a month. For a protected home on {{in.other_units|int}} units that raises the bill from {{out.before_rs|rs}} to {{out.after_rs|rs}}, {{out.extra_rs|rs}} more, because every unit moves to the unprotected {{out.after_rate|rs2}} rate. Losing protection then costs at least {{out.lock_extra_rs|rs}} over the next {{out.lock_months|int}} bills.
how: AC: {{out.avg_kw|2}} kW × {{out.hours}} hours = {{out.daily_units|1}} units a day; {{out.daily_units|1}} units × {{out.days}} days = {{out.ac_units|int}} units a month. Without the AC: {{out.other_units}} units on the {{out.before_category|raw}} tariff = {{out.before_rs|rs}}. With the AC: {{out.total_units|int}} units on the {{out.after_category|raw}} tariff (top slab rate {{out.after_rate|rs2}} per unit) = {{out.after_rs|rs}}, including fixed charge, surcharges and GST; an FPA counts only if you enter it. Extra: {{out.after_rs|rs}} − {{out.before_rs|rs}} = {{out.extra_rs|rs}}; {{out.extra_rs|rs}} ÷ {{out.ac_units|int}} AC units = {{out.rs_per_ac_unit|rs2}} for each unit the AC uses. Protection penalty: {{out.lock_months|int}} bills × {{out.lock_per_month|rs}} = {{out.lock_extra_rs|rs}}.
key_facts: What an AC adds to a Pakistani electricity bill is the bill with the AC minus the bill without it, not the AC's units × one slab rate, because the slab the whole home reaches sets the rate of every unit.
A {{out.ac_name|raw}} running {{in.hours|int}} hours a day for {{out.days|2}} days uses about {{out.ac_units|int}} units a month.

A protected home on {{in.other_units|int}} units pays about {{out.before_rs|rs}}; adding that AC takes it to {{out.total_units|int}} units at the unprotected {{out.after_rate|rs2}} rate, about {{out.after_rs|rs}}, so each AC unit really costs {{out.rs_per_ac_unit|rs2}}.

One month above {{out.protected_limit|int}} units ends protected status: the next {{out.lock_months|int}} bills are charged at unprotected rates even without the AC, at least {{out.lock_extra_rs|rs}} more in this example.

An unprotected home on {{ex.1.in.other_units|int}} units pays about {{ex.1.out.extra_rs|rs}} more a month for the same AC, {{ex.1.out.rs_per_ac_unit|rs2}} for each AC unit, because the total moves from the {{ex.1.out.before_rate|rs2}} slab to the {{ex.1.out.after_rate|rs2}} slab.

formula.text: Extra = Bill(other units + AC units) − Bill(other units); AC units = kW_avg × h × days
lines: Bill(units) = energy charge of the slab reached + fixed charge per sanctioned kW + FC surcharge + QTA + FPA, then GST (the electricity bill calculator's method)
kW_avg = the AC's average draw over an hour; h = AC hours a day; days = AC days in the month
A protected home whose total goes over the protected limit is billed at unprotected rates
Penalty = protected months × (Bill of the other units at unprotected rates − Bill of the other units at protected rates)

sections.h2: How much will an AC increase my electricity bill?
p: Take the bill without the AC and the bill with it, and subtract. With the defaults, a {{out.ac_name|raw}} running {{in.hours|int}} hours a day adds {{out.ac_units|int}} units to a home that used {{in.other_units|int}}. The bill goes from {{out.before_rs|rs}} to {{out.after_rs|rs}}, which is {{out.extra_rs|rs}} more a month, or {{out.rs_per_ac_unit|rs2}} for each unit the AC uses.

That is far above the {{out.after_rate|rs2}} slab rate, because the AC does not only add its own units: it re-prices the units the home was already using. An estimate that multiplies the AC's units by one rate misses this, so it reads too low exactly when it matters.

sections.h2: Why the AC pushes you into a higher slab
p: On the unprotected domestic tariff every unit is charged at the rate of the slab the monthly total reaches. An unprotected home on {{ex.1.in.other_units|int}} units pays {{ex.1.out.before_rate|rs2}} per unit; with the AC it reaches {{ex.1.out.total_units|int}} units and pays {{ex.1.out.after_rate|rs2}} on all of them. The bill rises by {{ex.1.out.extra_rs|rs}}, {{ex.1.out.rs_per_ac_unit|rs2}} for each AC unit.
The fixed charge per sanctioned kW also rises with the slab, and the per-unit surcharges and GST grow with the units, so the calculator prices the whole bill twice rather than adding one line.

sections.h2: Protected consumers: the six-month cost of one hot month
p: A home is protected only while each of its last {{out.lock_months|int}} bills stayed within {{out.protected_limit|int}} units. A single AC month above that limit moves the home to unprotected rates, and it stays there for the next {{out.lock_months|int}} bills even after the AC is switched off.

With the defaults the penalty on those later bills is {{out.lock_per_month|rs}} a month, {{out.lock_extra_rs|rs}} in all, on top of the {{out.extra_rs|rs}} extra in the AC month itself. It is a floor: summer bills with the AC running cost more. If your usage sits just under the limit, fewer AC hours can keep protection, as the third worked example shows.

sections.h2: How to bring the AC's cost down
p: Fewer units in the peak months is what counts: a higher set point, closed doors and curtains, and switching off when the room is empty. An inverter AC uses fewer units than a non-inverter AC of the same tonnage; the inverter AC payback calculator shows how long the price gap takes to recover, and the temperature saving calculator shows what a higher set point saves.

mistakes: Multiplying the AC's units by your current slab rate. The AC moves the whole bill to a higher slab, so the real extra is the difference of two full bills.
Forgetting the protected limit. One month over it costs the protected rates for the following bills too, not just that month.
Using a summer bill as the usage without the AC. Take a month when the AC was off, or the AC is counted twice.
Taking the AC's rated input as its average draw. An inverter AC averages well below its label once the room is cool.
safety: A new AC needs its own circuit with the right cable and MCB, and the home may need a higher sanctioned load. Have a licensed electrician check the wiring before installing it.

faq.q: How much does a 1.5 ton inverter AC add to the electricity bill?
faq.a: Running {{in.hours|int}} hours a day it adds about {{out.ac_units|int}} units a month. For a protected home on {{in.other_units|int}} units that is {{out.extra_rs|rs}} more a month; for an unprotected home on {{ex.1.in.other_units|int}} units, {{ex.1.out.extra_rs|rs}} more.

faq.q: Why is my bill so high after I started using the AC?
faq.a: Because the AC pushes the whole month into a higher slab or off the protected tariff, and every unit is then charged at the higher rate. In the default example each AC unit really costs {{out.rs_per_ac_unit|rs2}}.

faq.q: Will using an AC make me lose protected status?
faq.a: Yes, if the month's total goes over {{out.protected_limit|int}} units. Then the next {{out.lock_months|int}} bills are charged at unprotected rates even without the AC; in the default example that costs at least {{out.lock_extra_rs|rs}} more.

faq.q: How many hours can I run an AC and stay protected?
faq.a: Enter your usual units and lower the AC hours until the Protected status lost result shows No. A home on {{ex.2.in.other_units|int}} units stays protected with a {{ex.2.out.ac_name|raw}} for {{ex.2.in.hours|int}} hours a day.

faq.q: Is this the same as the AC running cost per month?
faq.a: No. The running cost is the AC's units × one rate. This calculator compares your whole bill with and without the AC, so it includes the slab jump, the fixed charge, surcharges and GST.

faq.q: Does it work for LESCO, IESCO, MEPCO and other DISCOs?
faq.a: Yes. Every DISCO uses the same national domestic tariff, and NEPRA sets one FPA for all of them; enter the month's FPA from your own bill under Advanced settings.
